Prevention: Leersia are considered to be the main weed host.
Use moderate amounts of fertilizer - 80-100 kg
N/ha is suggested, depending on local conditions.
Too much nitrogen increases shoot and leaf production and promotes disease development because of higher humidity.
When taking seedlings from the nursery ease them out gently with roots intact and do not clip leaves.
Damage could increase susceptibility to the disease.
Ensure good drainage of fields and nurseries.
Floodwater spreads the bacterial leaf blight between plants.
Only use plants without symptoms for seed production.
Monitoring: Seedlings: leaves show grey-green streaks starting from the tips and margins; later the streaks join together, turn yellowish-white with wavy edges, dry up and die.
Older leaves: pale yellow steaks with wavy margins from the tips towards the base.
Small milky drops of liquid (bacteria) ooze from the streaks on the leaves, later drying as a crust.
To check that bacteria are present in the leaves, cut a leaf across a young streak and place the cut end in a glass of water: if bacteria are present a cloudy liquid will stream out.
Streaks also occur on the leaf sheaths and the stems of susceptible varieties.
Bacterial leaf blight produces wavy leaf streaks whereas bacterial leaf blight produces wavy leaf streaks.
Squeeze the low part of the plant - if a yellow liquid oozes from the ends of cut leaves, the cause is bacterial leaf blight and not stem borer damage.
Direct Control: Plough land to bury rice stubble, straw, rattoon plants and volunteer seedlings.
Bacteria causing this disease do not live long in the soil.
